pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Compare and order two-digit numbers using >, =, < based on PLACE VALUE: compare the tens first, and only if the tens are equal compare the ones. A procedural skill built directly on tens-and-ones understanding.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'compare and order numbers from 0 up to 100; use <, > and = signs'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.3 'compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results with the symbols >, =, and <'.
• Operational details — Establish the meaning of each symbol before speed ('the open mouth eats the bigger number' is a crutch; ground it in 'greater than/less than' with quantities). Teach the leading-digit rule explicitly: compare tens, decide; if tens tie, compare ones. Use base-ten blocks or a number line so 'bigger' is a seen quantity/position, not a guess. Progress from comparing pairs to ordering a set (smallest→largest and largest→smallest).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): place > or < between two numbers with clearly different tens (34, 52) and justify by the tens. Tier B (age 6-7): compare a same-tens pair (34, 38) by the ones and place the correct symbol. Tier C (age 7): order a mixed set of five two-digit numbers and explain the tens-then-ones rule, including a same-tens tie.
bestPractices: Compare quantities and positions FIRST (blocks side by side, points on a 0-100 line) so 'greater' means visibly more, then attach the symbol — symbol before meaning breeds the crocodile-mouth-without-understanding error.
Teach the leading-digit strategy explicitly: look at the tens; the number with more tens is greater; only if the tens are equal do you compare the ones.
Read the statement both ways — 34 < 43 as 'thirty-four is less than forty-three' AND 43 > 34 — so the child sees the relation is the same fact stated from either end.
Use same-tens pairs (34 vs 38) deliberately to force attention onto the ones once tens are equal, defeating 'just compare the first digit'.
Move from pairwise comparison to ordering a set, recording with symbols, so comparison becomes a tool for organising numbers, not an isolated trick.
keyRepresentations: Two sets of base-ten blocks placed side by side (more tens = taller/greater)
0-100 number line where the number further right is greater
Tens|ones place-value chart aligning two numbers column by column
The <, >, = symbols with the 'points to the smaller / opens to the larger' orientation, grounded in quantity
Ordered track or 'washing line' for pegging a set of numbers smallest to largest
commonMisconceptions: Using the crocodile/Pac-Man mouth as a rote trick with no sense of which number is actually bigger, so the symbol is placed by guess.
Comparing by digit count of the numeral or by the ONES first (34 vs 38: choosing by 4 vs 8 alone is fine here, but 52 vs 48 wrongly judged by 2 vs 8) — ignoring the leading (tens) digit.
Reversing the symbol — knowing which is bigger but writing > where < belongs.
Thinking = can only sit between identical-looking expressions, not that it asserts equal value.
For same-tens pairs, defaulting to 'they're the same' because the tens match, instead of moving to the ones.

learn.summary: Ages 6-7 (Y2) compare and order two-digit numbers using >, =, < grounded in place value: compare the tens first, and only if the tens are equal compare the ones. Establish quantity/position meaning of 'greater' and 'less' with base-ten blocks and a 0-100 number line before attaching symbols, deliberately use same-tens pairs to force attention onto the ones, and progress from comparing pairs to ordering a set in both directions.

activities.title: Comparison bench: build, see, and place the symbol
feedback: If the symbol is placed correctly, confirm by showing the greater pile 'winning' or the line marker leaning toward the larger number: the wide open side faces the larger number, the point faces the smaller.

If the symbol is reversed but the reasoning is right ('43 is bigger' yet < is written), separate the two steps: praise the correct comparison, then re-anchor the orientation — open side toward the larger number — and have them re-read the whole statement aloud to check.
If 'greater' is guessed from the numeral shape (e.g. 'longer looks bigger'), return to the blocks/line so 'greater' is a seen quantity, then re-attach the symbol.
activities.rationale: Comparison becomes meaningful when two quantities are shown as blocks and as points on a line before a symbol is attached, so 'greater' is visibly more rather than a guess. Showing both forms and reading the statement both ways grounds the symbols in quantity and treats the relation as a single reversible fact. An optional live version (dragging the symbol into the gap with the greater pile lighting up and the line marker leaning) makes the mechanism concrete, but the core learning works with physical blocks and a drawn line.
sourceClaims: 1.NBT.3: compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording with >, =, <.
Grounding comparison symbols in quantity/position and teaching a tens-then-ones leading-digit strategy prevents rote crocodile-mouth errors.
learnerActions: Build or show two two-digit numbers in two forms at once: base-ten block piles and dots/markers on a shared 0-100 number line.

Decide which is greater by looking at the quantity/position first (more tens rods and more blocks in total, further right on the line), then say it aloud: e.g. 'forty-three is greater than thirty-four'.
Place the correct symbol (<, >, or =) into the gap between the two numbers.
Read the completed statement both ways: 34 < 43 ('thirty-four is less than forty-three') and 43 > 34 ('forty-three is greater than thirty-four').
State the rule used: compare the tens first; the number with more tens is greater, and if the tens are equal, compare the ones.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Greater' and 'less' name a real difference in quantity/position, and the symbol records that relation — the same fact can be read from either end.

activities.title: Tens-tie rounds: when the first digit can't decide
feedback: If the child says a same-tens pair is 'the same' because the tens match, prompt them to move on to the ones: 3 tens and 4 ones versus 3 tens and 8 ones.
For 52 vs 48, if the child picks 48 as larger because 8 > 2, rebuild both with tens and ones so that five tens clearly outweigh four tens; the ones only matter once the tens tie.
For 60 and 60, if the child hesitates to use =, confirm that = means equal value and both quantities match exactly.
activities.rationale: Same-tens pairs deliberately force attention onto the ones once the tens are equal, defeating the 'just compare the first digit' error; crossed-decade pairs (e.g. 52 vs 48) expose the ones-first misconception directly. An optional auto-generated 'tens tie' mode makes these cases frequent, but a teacher-chosen set of pairs serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Grounding comparison symbols in quantity/position and teaching a tens-then-ones leading-digit strategy prevents rote crocodile-mouth errors.
1.NBT.3: compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording with >, =, <.
learnerActions: Compare same-tens pairs such as 34 and 38, where the tens columns are identical.
Notice that the tens no longer settle it, then compare the ones to decide which is greater.
Place the correct symbol and justify: 'the tens are the same, so I looked at the ones'.
Try a 'crossed-decade' pair such as 52 and 48, and check: 52 has more tens, so it is greater even though its ones digit (2) is smaller than 8.
Also handle an equal pair such as 60 and 60, choosing = and explaining that both show the same value.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing only the first digit you see is not enough: compare the tens first, and only when the tens are equal does the ones digit decide. = asserts equal value, not merely identical-looking symbols.

activities.title: Order a scrambled set onto a washing line
feedback: If a number with a large ones digit is placed too high (e.g. 19 above 51), rebuild both with blocks so 51's five tens stand against 19's single ten, then re-place.
If ordering is correct one way but shaky the other, have the child read the finished line aloud in both directions to confirm it is the same facts reversed.
Confirm a correct order by checking each neighbouring pair with a symbol.
activities.rationale: Moving from pairwise comparison to ordering a set, recording with symbols, makes comparison a practical tool and surfaces whether tens genuinely govern the child's decisions. An ordering mode where numbers are dragged onto a washing line and checked left-to-right is one concrete way to do this; pegged cards on a string work equally well.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of two-digit numbers, e.g. 19, 27, 51, 72, and arrange them smallest to largest.
Repeat, ordering the same set largest to smallest.
Include a set containing a same-tens tie so ordering requires the ones to break it.
Check the finished order left to right and record the relations with symbols where appropriate.
Explain how you decided the order: tens first across the set, ones to break ties.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparison is a tool for organising numbers: ordering a set applies the tens-then-ones rule repeatedly, not as an isolated trick.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'how do you know?'
feedback: If the child explains correctly but writes the symbol backwards, treat orientation as a separate, fixable step and re-read the statement aloud.
If the child cannot say why the tens were examined first, return to blocks to re-establish that a ten is worth more than a one.
activities.rationale: A short Socratic probe on a tricky same-tens or crossed-decade pair may elicit and correct compare-the-tens-first reasoning and catch the ones-first error. Talking out the reasoning complements the hands-on and symbol-placing practice; it is offered alongside that work rather than as a substitute for it.
sourceClaims: Grounding comparison symbols in quantity/position and teaching a tens-then-ones leading-digit strategy prevents rote crocodile-mouth errors.
learnerActions: Explain aloud which digit you looked at first and why, on a tricky pair such as 52 and 48.
Answer: '34 and 43 use the same two digits — how can one be bigger?' by referring to place value.
Decide and justify the symbol for an equal pair like 60 and 60.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a comparison out loud reveals and corrects the reasoning (tens first, ones to break a tie) behind the written symbol.

activities.title: Consolidation and check: choose, order, fill the gap
feedback: For a wrong symbol, ask the child to identify which is greater first, then fix the orientation separately.
For a mis-ordered set, direct attention to the tens across the whole set before the ones.
activities.rationale: Comparison and ordering map cleanly onto choose-the-symbol, order-the-set, and fill-the-gap tasks, making this a natural consolidation and check surface. These tasks drill and check the skill; on their own they do not build the underlying quantity sense, so they should follow the block/line and tens-tie work rather than replace it.
learnerActions: Choose the correct symbol between two numbers, including a same-tens item and an item designed to tempt symbol reversal.
Order a scrambled set smallest to largest.
Fill in the missing symbol in a statement and read it back aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: The tens-then-ones comparison and correct symbol use can be applied quickly and reliably across varied pairs and sets.

constraints: Establish the meaning of each symbol with quantities/positions before pushing for speed; 'the open mouth eats the bigger number' is only a memory crutch and must be grounded in 'greater than / less than' with real quantities.
Treat recognition and drill tasks (choosing or filling a symbol) as consolidation/check; they verify the skill but do not by themselves build quantity sense or independent reasoning.

A single fixed illustration can anchor the tens-then-ones rule with one worked pair, but on its own it cannot let the child compare varied pairs or order a set, which is where the skill is practised; use it as an anchor, not the main activity.
Keep symbol orientation (open side to the larger number) as a separate check from the greater/less reasoning, so a correct comparison written with a reversed symbol is diagnosed accurately.
Base-ten blocks and the drawn number line are physical representations with slight thickness; they stand for the abstract numerical values being compared, not the values themselves.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source noted CCSS alignment as 1.NBT.3 (Grade 1) while targeting UK Y2 (ages 6-7); the standards citations are from different jurisdictions/grades and were preserved as written, not independently reconfirmed.

The source's error-pattern note '34 vs 38: choosing by 4 vs 8 alone is fine here, but 52 vs 48 wrongly judged by 2 vs 8' is accurate: when tens are equal the ones decide, but when tens differ the ones must not. Activities make this distinction explicit (crossed-decade pairs) so learners do not over-generalise 'compare the first/last digit'.

The original claimed a static picture 'can only show one fixed pair', that 3D 'adds no comparative information', and that the judgement is 'better trained by manipulating symbols than by talking'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources, so they were softened to scoped statements about what fixed images, drill tasks and dialogue do and do not do here.

The UK NC claim and CCSS 1.NBT.3 establish the topic/standard; the UK NC claim was not attached to any activity's sourceClaims because it supports the curriculum requirement (preserved in summary/constraints) rather than a specific pedagogical principle in a rationale.

Two of three cited sources were marked verified:false in the source row; their claims were retained only where they directly support a stated teaching principle, and claims that only establish the topic/standard were not used to justify specific pedagogical moves.

probeDeeper: Which digit did you look at first — tens or ones? Why the tens?
34 and 43 use the same two digits — how can one be bigger?
Put a symbol between 60 and 60 — which one, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 34 < 43; order 19, 27, 51, 72; and they compare the tens digit first, ones only to break a tie.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares by a single digit's size regardless of place: thinks 19 > 51 because 9 > 1
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build both with tens and ones; establish that tens are worth more, so compare tens first. Re-order with the models in view.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ordering puts numbers with a big ones digit too high; 34/43 judged by the shared digits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the < / > symbol — opens it toward the smaller number
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the symbol: the open (wide) side faces the larger number, the point faces the smaller. Read the whole statement aloud to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasoning is right ('43 is bigger') but the symbol written points the wrong way.

responseLevels.gap: Orders by a single digit ignoring place, or the symbol is reversed with no place reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Compares and orders two-digit numbers by tens-then-ones, writes >, <, = correctly, and justifies by place value.
responseLevels.partial: Compares correctly for clearly different numbers but stumbles on same-digit pairs, or reasons right yet writes the symbol backwards.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch them compare and order. 'Put the right symbol between 34 and 43. Now order these smallest to largest: 27, 72, 19, 51. Tell me how you decided.' The 34/43 pair (same digits) is the key — watch whether they weigh the tens first.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 34 vs 43 uses identical digits so a child comparing digit-by-digit without place weighting cannot fake it; ordering a mixed set reveals whether tens govern the comparison. The '<'/'>' choice also exposes pure symbol reversal separately from the reasoning.
